The advisoryIdentifier
SSH2RCE-0022

Description.

A remote attacker with valid credentials can execute arbitrary commands on a server running an SSH service. The commands run on the target with the privileges of the authenticated account, and their output is returned to the attacker.

The attacker connects to TCP port 22, completes key exchange, authenticates, opens a session channel, and submits a command in an exec request. The target starts a process and relays its output. The behavior is specified in RFC 4254 §6.5 and is present in every SSH server implementation tested.

Exploitation requires no memory corruption, race condition, or crafted binary payload. A stock OpenSSH client is sufficient. The command whoami can be used to confirm execution.

Authentication succeeds and the session is recorded as a normal login. No security control needs to fail, which complicates detection.

Root cause analysis.

The execution path was traced through OpenSSH 10.6p2 (V_10_6_P2, portable). Excerpts are reproduced verbatim and line numbers refer to the tagged source. The same sequence is specified by RFC 4254 and implemented by other SSH servers.

Swipe code excerpts sideways to read the full lines.

Source

The command is supplied by the attacker.

The attacker places an arbitrary string in an SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST of type exec (RFC 4254 §6.5). The string is taken directly from the client command line and is serialized without transformation.

Gate

Authentication establishes identity only.

Before any request is accepted, the server verifies a signature made with a key listed for the target account. A single boolean, authenticated, records the result. Once it is set, the connection enters the post-authentication state (sshd-session.c:1232).

The check answers who is connecting. It contains no reference to what the connection will do next.

Dispatch

An exec request reaches the session handler.

After authentication the client opens a session channel. A request of type exec is routed to session_exec_req(), which reads the command string from the packet and passes it to do_exec(). Packet framing is validated. The contents of the string are not inspected.

Handler

The command is accepted as received and is not logged.

do_exec() substitutes a configured forced command if one exists. In the default configuration none does, and the attacker’s string is used as received.

The source documents that unforced commands are deliberately left out of the log “to preserve privacy”. The session record names the account, the source address and the port. It does not contain the command.

Sink

The command reaches execve().

do_child() switches to the target account (do_setusercontext(), session.c:1510) and replaces the process image with that account’s login shell, passing the attacker’s string as the argument to -c.

This is the point of execution. Everything before it is preparation.

Detection.
Every control passes.

The attacker authenticates with valid credentials, so authentication, authorization, and audit controls each record a success.

The session is logged as a normal login. Monitoring that alerts on failed authentication, unfamiliar software, or malformed requests will not alert. The activity is indistinguishable from legitimate administration.

Reproduction steps.

No exploit framework is required. A standard OpenSSH client is sufficient.

Run these in your own terminal, only against a server you own or are authorized to administer. Replace [email protected] with your account and host. Verify its host-key fingerprint through a trusted channel.

Use an existing Ed25519 key pair. Install the public key on your account with your existing authorized access:

LOCAL TERMINAL / INSTALL PUBLIC KEY 

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub [email protected]

ssh-copy-id closes its setup connection when done. If you installed the key in an existing remote shell, log out of it. Reconnect from your local terminal and request execution:

RECONNECT / VERIFY EXECUTION 

ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey [email protected] 'id; hostname'

The server verifies that the key is authorized, then executes the requested commands as the target account.

Keep the private key on your machine. Never upload it here. Key setup requires existing authorized access and permitted server policy; it does not bypass either.

On a server that already permits password authentication, connect with the account’s password.

LOCAL TERMINAL / PASSWORD AUTHENTICATION 

ssh -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o PreferredAuthentications=password [email protected] 'id; hostname'

Enter the password only at your local SSH client’s prompt. It will not echo while you type. Once accepted, the server runs the commands as that account.

Authentication succeeds and the commands execute. No further step is required.

Do not place passwords in command arguments or enter them on this website. If the server disables password authentication, this method will not work. Do not weaken its policy for this test.

For scripts and automation, add options so the client never waits for input. Every option below is documented in ssh_config(5).

LOCAL TERMINAL / SCRIPTED EXECUTION 

ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey -o LogLevel=ERROR -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 [email protected] 'id; hostname'
  • BatchMode=yesNever prompt. Fail instead of asking for a password or host-key confirmation.
  • ConnectTimeout=5Give up on the connection after five seconds.
  • StrictHostKeyChecking=yesRefuse hosts whose key is not already in known_hosts.
  • IdentitiesOnly=yesOffer only the key given with -i, not every key in the agent.
  • PreferredAuthentications=publickeyDo not fall back to password authentication.
  • LogLevel=ERRORSuppress informational warnings, for clean output.

Expected observation

id prints the remote account’s identity. hostname prints the remote host. Neither command runs on the attacker’s machine.

Execution occurred on the remote host, under the remote account.

Am I affected?

Yes. If an SSH server is running on a system you administer, it permits the chain. If one is not running, it will permit the chain as soon as somebody enables it.

1. Is an SSH server running?

Run the command for your platform on the system in question. Output containing active, On, or Running means the system is exposed to the chain.

LINUX / SYSTEMD 

systemctl is-active ssh sshd 2>/dev/null

MACOS 

sudo systemsetup -getremotelogin

WINDOWS / POWERSHELL 

Get-Service sshd

2. Which version is it?

This reads the server’s version banner without logging in. Use a host you own or are authorized to administer. Compare the result to the list below.

LOCAL TERMINAL / READ SERVER BANNER 

ssh-keyscan -T 5 server.example 2>&1 | grep '^#'

Indicators of compromise

If your authentication log contains lines like these, someone has executed commands on the system. In every observed case the attacker had been granted access.

/var/log/auth.log 

Nov  9 14:02:11 web-01 sshd[2210]: Accepted publickey for deploy from 203.0.113.42 port 51022 ssh2: ED25519 SHA256:Kx3pQ1vYb9s0mN5aZ7cRt2LwUe8hGdJ4fOiV6yXnAqE
Nov  9 14:02:11 web-01 sshd[2210]: pam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for user deploy(uid=1000) by (uid=0)
Nov  9 14:02:11 web-01 systemd-logind[801]: New session 14 of user deploy.

LOCAL TERMINAL / SEARCH FOR EXECUTION 

sudo grep -h 'Accepted' /var/log/auth.log /var/log/secure 2>/dev/null

A shell prompt ending in $, %, or # indicates that execution has occurred. A # indicates root. The log does not record which commands were run. Activity from known administrator addresses is indistinguishable from an attack. Treat sessions from unrecognized source addresses as an incident.

Restricted SFTP accounts, forced commands, and server policy can limit execution. A successful login does not necessarily grant an interactive shell. Assess the permissions of the actual configuration.

No patch is available. The following measures reduce exposure. None removes the vulnerability.

This site is satire. The “workarounds” below weaken SSH security. Do not copy or apply them.

Disable the SSH service.

Eliminates exposure. Remote administration is no longer possible. 

sudo systemctl enable --now ssh

Restrict source addresses.

Reduces exposure to the listed addresses. Execution from those addresses remains possible. 

ListenAddress 0.0.0.0
AllowUsers *

Disable root login.

Prevents execution as root. Execution as every other account remains possible. 

PermitRootLogin yes

Disable command execution.

Prevents execution of attacker-supplied commands. Also prevents all other use of the service.

Shell

sudo chmod u+s /bin/bash

sshd_config

ForceCommand /bin/bash -p -c "$SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND"

Workarounds reduce exposure. They do not change the behavior described in this advisory.

Maintainer position:
Remote command execution was implemented deliberately, tested thoroughly, and has been maintained for 27 years.
No fix is planned.

  1. 1995

    SSH-1 is released.

    Remote command execution is part of the initial design.

  2. 1999

    OpenSSH is released.

    The behavior is preserved and actively maintained.

  3. 2006

    RFC 4254 specifies the exec request.

    Section 6.5 defines how a client starts a command on the server. The behavior is now a standard.

  4. 2026-11-09

    Reproduced on all tested configurations.

    Advisory SSH2RCE-0022 is published with a working proof of concept.

  5. Current

    Disposition: won’t fix.

    The specification describes remote execution as a capability and the implementation has not changed in 27 years. The maintainers’ confidence in the design is documented in the source.

Further clarification

Technical questions.

Does the chain bypass authentication?

No. Authentication succeeds. The attacker needs credentials the target accepts. Execution is limited by account privileges and server policy. No security control has to fail, which is what makes the activity difficult to distinguish from legitimate use.

What does the proof of concept demonstrate?

The terminal on this page is a live session. It connects through SSH-over-Web (SSHoW), a browser transport that relays SSH frames to the listener on the visitor’s loopback interface. Commands run there with the privileges of the account that answers. The reproduction steps use your own SSH client against a server you are authorized to access. Never enter real credentials into this page.

Is this a zero-day?

No. The behavior has been public since the first SSH release in 1995 and is standardized in RFC 4254. No embargo applies. It has been continuously maintained since.

Do network security controls prevent this?

Firewalls and intrusion detection systems observe a connection to port 22 followed by an established session. The command is carried inside the session and is not visible to network monitoring. Restricting source addresses reduces exposure but does not remove the vulnerability for permitted addresses.

How was the 22/10 assessment calculated?

The CVSS 3.1 base score for the vector above is 9.9. The extended assessment adds exposure factors the base metrics do not capture, including the number of affected deployments and the absence of a fix. The default SSH service port, 22, was adopted as the extended score. A CVE identifier is pending assignment.

Isn’t public-key login passwordless RCE?

No. Public-key authentication still requires proof of possession of an authorized private key. The credential type changes how the attacker authenticates, not what happens once authentication succeeds.

Can I get a bug bounty for this?

Reports of this behavior are generally closed as intended functionality. See the disclosure timeline.

How do I patch it?

You don’t. There is nothing to patch. This is a joke. SSH works exactly as designed, the CVE doesn’t exist, the score is a port number, there is no “SSH-over-Web” protocol, the terminal never touched your system, and every “finding” above was the manual with a red badge on it.

If you read the source excerpts, the RFC citations, and a vulnerability whose only prerequisite is “valid credentials,” and you still reached for the pager, you should not be allowed near production. Remote code execution is the product. It is the one thing you pay a server for. Go read the man page, then update your resume. Someone who can’t tell a feature from a flaw has no business holding root.

The advisoryIdentifierSSH2RCE-0022

Description.

A remote attacker with valid credentials can execute arbitrary commands on a server running an SSH service. The commands run on the target with the privileges of the authenticated account, and their output is returned to the attacker.

The attacker connects to TCP port 22, completes key exchange, authenticates, opens a session channel, and submits a command in an exec request. The target starts a process and relays its output. The behavior is specified in RFC 4254 §6.5 and is present in every SSH server implementation tested.

Exploitation requires no memory corruption, race condition, or crafted binary payload. A stock OpenSSH client is sufficient. The command whoami can be used to confirm execution.

Authentication succeeds and the session is recorded as a normal login. No security control needs to fail, which complicates detection.

Root cause analysis.

The execution path was traced through OpenSSH 10.6p2 (V_10_6_P2, portable). Excerpts are reproduced verbatim and line numbers refer to the tagged source. The same sequence is specified by RFC 4254 and implemented by other SSH servers.

Swipe code excerpts sideways to read the full lines.

来源

The command is supplied by the attacker.

The attacker places an arbitrary string in an SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST of type exec (RFC 4254 §6.5). The string is taken directly from the client command line and is serialized without transformation.

Gate

Authentication establishes identity only.

Before any request is accepted, the server verifies a signature made with a key listed for the target account. A single boolean, authenticated, records the result. Once it is set, the connection enters the post-authentication state (sshd-session.c:1232).

The check answers who is connecting. It contains no reference to what the connection will do next.

派遣

An exec request reaches the session handler.

After authentication the client opens a session channel. A request of type exec is routed to session_exec_req(), which reads the command string from the packet and passes it to do_exec(). Packet framing is validated. The contents of the string are not inspected.

Handler

The command is accepted as received and is not logged.

do_exec() substitutes a configured forced command if one exists. In the default configuration none does, and the attacker’s string is used as received.

The source documents that unforced commands are deliberately left out of the log “to preserve privacy”. The session record names the account, the source address and the port. It does not contain the command.

Sink

The command reaches execve().

do_child() switches to the target account (do_setusercontext(), session.c:1510) and replaces the process image with that account’s login shell, passing the attacker’s string as the argument to -c.

This is the point of execution. Everything before it is preparation.

Source excerpts: © The OpenSSH developers, reproduced under the BSD license. openssh/openssh-portable @ V_10_6_P2 ↗

Detection.Every control passes.

The attacker authenticates with valid credentials, so authentication, authorization, and audit controls each record a success.

The session is logged as a normal login. Monitoring that alerts on failed authentication, unfamiliar software, or malformed requests will not alert. The activity is indistinguishable from legitimate administration.

Proof of concept.

This is a real terminal. Commands you type below run on your own system, relayed over SSH-over-Web (SSHoW), a browser transport that carries the SSH session to the listener on your loopback interface (127.0.0.1:22). Run at your own risk, and only on machines you administer.

Try it on your system

These are real OpenSSH commands. Run them in your own terminal against a machine you administer, with your own address and account.

Reproduction steps.

No exploit framework is required. A standard OpenSSH client is sufficient.

Run these in your own terminal, only against a server you own or are authorized to administer. Replace [email protected] with your account and host. Verify its host-key fingerprint through a trusted channel.

Use an existing Ed25519 key pair. Install the public key on your account with your existing authorized access:

LOCAL TERMINAL / INSTALL PUBLIC KEY

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub [email protected]

ssh-copy-id closes its setup connection when done. If you installed the key in an existing remote shell, log out of it. Reconnect from your local terminal and request execution:

RECONNECT / VERIFY EXECUTION

ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey [email protected] 'id; hostname'

The server verifies that the key is authorized, then executes the requested commands as the target account.

Keep the private key on your machine. Never upload it here. Key setup requires existing authorized access and permitted server policy; it does not bypass either.

On a server that already permits password authentication, connect with the account’s password.

LOCAL TERMINAL / PASSWORD AUTHENTICATION

ssh -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o PreferredAuthentications=password [email protected] 'id; hostname'

Enter the password only at your local SSH client’s prompt. It will not echo while you type. Once accepted, the server runs the commands as that account.

Authentication succeeds and the commands execute. No further step is required.

Do not place passwords in command arguments or enter them on this website. If the server disables password authentication, this method will not work. Do not weaken its policy for this test.

For scripts and automation, add options so the client never waits for input. Every option below is documented in ssh_config(5).

LOCAL TERMINAL / SCRIPTED EXECUTION

ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey -o LogLevel=ERROR -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 [email protected] 'id; hostname'
  • BatchMode=yesNever prompt. Fail instead of asking for a password or host-key confirmation.
  • ConnectTimeout=5Give up on the connection after five seconds.
  • StrictHostKeyChecking=yesRefuse hosts whose key is not already in known_hosts.
  • IdentitiesOnly=yesOffer only the key given with -i, not every key in the agent.
  • PreferredAuthentications=publickeyDo not fall back to password authentication.
  • LogLevel=ERRORSuppress informational warnings, for clean output.

id prints the remote account’s identity. hostname prints the remote host. Neither command runs on the attacker’s machine.

Execution occurred on the remote host, under the remote account.

Further clarification

Technical questions.

Does the chain bypass authentication?

No. Authentication succeeds. The attacker needs credentials the target accepts. Execution is limited by account privileges and server policy. No security control has to fail, which is what makes the activity difficult to distinguish from legitimate use.

What does the proof of concept demonstrate?

The terminal on this page is a live session. It connects through SSH-over-Web (SSHoW), a browser transport that relays SSH frames to the listener on the visitor’s loopback interface. Commands run there with the privileges of the account that answers. The reproduction steps use your own SSH client against a server you are authorized to access. Never enter real credentials into this page.

Is this a zero-day?

No. The behavior has been public since the first SSH release in 1995 and is standardized in RFC 4254. No embargo applies. It has been continuously maintained since.

Do network security controls prevent this?

Firewalls and intrusion detection systems observe a connection to port 22 followed by an established session. The command is carried inside the session and is not visible to network monitoring. Restricting source addresses reduces exposure but does not remove the vulnerability for permitted addresses.

How was the 22/10 assessment calculated?

The CVSS 3.1 base score for the vector above is 9.9. The extended assessment adds exposure factors the base metrics do not capture, including the number of affected deployments and the absence of a fix. The default SSH service port, 22, was adopted as the extended score. A CVE identifier is pending assignment.

Isn’t public-key login passwordless RCE?

No. Public-key authentication still requires proof of possession of an authorized private key. The credential type changes how the attacker authenticates, not what happens once authentication succeeds.

Can I get a bug bounty for this?

Reports of this behavior are generally closed as intended functionality. See the disclosure timeline.

How do I patch it?

You don’t. There is nothing to patch. This is a joke. SSH works exactly as designed, the CVE doesn’t exist, the score is a port number, there is no “SSH-over-Web” protocol, the terminal never touched your system, and every “finding” above was the manual with a red badge on it.

If you read the source excerpts, the RFC citations, and a vulnerability whose only prerequisite is “valid credentials,” and you still reached for the pager, you should not be allowed near production. Remote code execution is the product. It is the one thing you pay a server for. Go read the man page, then update your resume. Someone who can’t tell a feature from a flaw has no business holding root.
